note: CKEditor Plugin Report is a single read-only admin report. Route ckeditor_plugin_report.plugin_report at /admin/reports/ckeditor-plugins (under system.admin_reports), gated by the permission 'view ckeditor plugin report' (restrict access: true). Controller PluginReportController::content reads plugin.manager.ckeditor5.plugin (NULL_ON_INVALID_REFERENCE) and tabulates getDefinitions() into columns Plugin ID / Provider / Class. No configure route, no config schema, no plugins/services/Drush of its own. The only persistent, mutable state relevant to the module is which roles hold the 'view ckeditor plugin report' permission (user.role.* config), so medium introspection reads that back and hard execution grants it. All fixtures use ckpr_-prefixed roles.

evals.prompt: I installed ckeditor_plugin_report. What is the URL path of the report it adds, and which permission controls access to it?
evals.expected_output: The report is at /admin/reports/ckeditor-plugins (route ckeditor_plugin_report.plugin_report, under the Reports menu) and is gated by the 'view ckeditor plugin report' permission.

evals.prompt: What information does the ckeditor_plugin_report page display for each CKEditor plugin, and which plugin manager does it read to build the list?
evals.expected_output: It reads the CKEditor 5 plugin manager (plugin.manager.ckeditor5.plugin) getDefinitions() and shows a table with three columns per plugin: Plugin ID, Provider (module), and Class.

evals.prompt: Why would a site administrator use ckeditor_plugin_report, for example when moving from CKEditor 4 to CKEditor 5?
evals.expected_output: It gives a full inventory of registered CKEditor 5 plugins (ID, provider module, class), useful for auditing which module supplies a plugin and for planning a CKEditor 4 -> 5 upgrade.

evals.prompt: On this Drupal site, one custom role has been granted access to the CKEditor plugin report. Inspect the live configuration and give the machine name of the role that holds the 'view ckeditor plugin report' permission.
evals.expected_output: The role ckpr_reviewer has the 'view ckeditor plugin report' permission (user.role.ckpr_reviewer permissions list includes it).

evals.prompt: This site has two custom roles, ckpr_yes and ckpr_no. Exactly one of them can open the CKEditor plugin report. Inspect the live role configuration and state which role can view the report.
evals.expected_output: ckpr_yes can view it: user.role.ckpr_yes has the 'view ckeditor plugin report' permission while ckpr_no does not.

evals.prompt: On this Drupal site there is a role with machine name ckpr_task that currently cannot access the CKEditor plugin report. Grant that role the permission needed to view the ckeditor_plugin_report page, and apply the change to the live site.
evals.expected_output: The user.role.ckpr_task config lists the 'view ckeditor plugin report' permission (e.g. $role->grantPermission('view ckeditor plugin report')->save()).

evals.prompt: Create a new Drupal role with machine name ckpr_build and give it exactly the permission required to open the CKEditor plugin report (the /admin/reports/ckeditor-plugins page from ckeditor_plugin_report). Save it to the live site.
evals.expected_output: A user.role.ckpr_build config entity exists and its permissions include 'view ckeditor plugin report'.
